Durrett presents the sphere example as 'Example 4.1.8. Borel's paradox' (p. 210): X a randomly chosen point on the earth; at first glance, if X is uniform on the globe, theta and the angle phi on the great circle should both be uniform; theta is uniform but phi is not; the paradox evaporates because in the new or the traditional formulation phi is independent of theta, so the conditional distribution is the unconditional one, which is not uniform since there is more land near the equator than near the North Pole. The route gives the model, the independence and the densities, but omits the name and attribution 'Borel's paradox', the naive expectation that both angles are uniform, and the source's resolution with its justification (more surface near the equator than near the poles); the regular-conditional-laws chapter never names the paradox. Supply the source's framing and justificatory claim. It does not count as coverage: the only treatment is in the unrouted owned file handbook/parts/p15/probability-spaces-and-random-variables-w02c-p15-002.tex (with its annex), which handbook/parts/p15.tex and handbook/annex/p15.tex do not \input; route pending, to be re-assessed after routing (lines 659-724).

Durrett (p. 214) states that regular conditional distributions do not always exist, that the first example was due to Dieudonne (1948), refers to Doob (1953), p. 624, and Faden (1985), and explains the difficulty: for disjoint A1, A2, ... the identity P(X in U An | G) = sum P(X in An | G) holds only almost surely, and if S contains enough countable collections of disjoint sets the exceptional sets may pile up. The route records only that such distributions need not exist (conditioning-independence-and-information-w02b-p15-008.tex lines 235-239) and this boundary limits the existence claim to the standard Borel class; the historical attribution with its references and the source's explanation of why existence can fail appear nowhere on the route. Supply them.
